Lending Club Loan Data Analysis¶

Deep Learning with Keras and TensorFlow — Course-End Project¶

Domain: Finance Objective: Build a deep learning model that predicts whether a loan will default, using Lending Club's historical loan data (2007-2015).

This notebook follows the four required tasks in order: (1) feature transformation, (2) exploratory data analysis, (3) additional feature engineering (correlation-based feature reduction), (4) deep learning modeling with Keras/TensorFlow.

purpose is the only categorical (text) column in the dataset — it has 7 discrete values with no natural order, so we one-hot encode it into separate binary columns, which is the standard way to turn an unordered categorical variable into numerical (discrete) features a neural network can use.

In [5]:
df_transformed = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['purpose'], drop_first=True)

# Convert the new one-hot columns from bool to int (0/1) for clarity
purpose_cols = [c for c in df_transformed.columns if c.startswith('purpose_')]
df_transformed[purpose_cols] = df_transformed[purpose_cols].astype(int)

print(f"Shape after transformation: {df_transformed.shape}")

2. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

2a. Target class balance¶

In [6]:
plt.figure(figsize=(6,5))
sns.countplot(data=df, x='not.fully.paid', hue='not.fully.paid', palette='Set2', legend=False)
plt.title('Target Distribution (0 = Fully Paid, 1 = Not Fully Paid / Default)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('lc_target_distribution.png', dpi=120)
plt.show()

print(df['not.fully.paid'].value_counts(normalize=True).round(4))

not.fully.paid
0    0.8399
1    0.1601
Name: proportion, dtype: float64

Class imbalance: about 16% of loans in this dataset were not fully paid. Less extreme than some credit datasets, but still meaningfully imbalanced — a model predicting "fully paid" for every loan would already be ~84% accurate while catching zero defaults, so accuracy alone won't be a reliable evaluation metric here (addressed further in Section 4).

2b. Distributions of key numeric factors¶

In [7]:
numeric_features = ['int.rate', 'installment', 'log.annual.inc', 'dti', 'fico',
                     'days.with.cr.line', 'revol.bal', 'revol.util']

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(18, 8))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flatten(), numeric_features):
    sns.histplot(df[col], kde=True, ax=ax, color='steelblue')
    ax.set_title(col)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('lc_feature_distributions.png', dpi=120)
plt.show()

Reading: fico is roughly normal, centered in the high-600s to low-700s. int.rate, dti, and installment are all right-skewed, reflecting the smaller number of higher-risk, higher-rate, higher-payment loans typical of a credit portfolio. revol.bal is heavily right-skewed with a long tail of large revolving balances, and log.annual.inc (already log-transformed in the source data) is close to normal, confirming the log transform did its job.

2c. How key factors relate to default¶

In [8]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 9))
compare_features = ['fico', 'int.rate', 'dti', 'revol.util', 'inq.last.6mths', 'installment']
for ax, col in zip(axes.flatten(), compare_features):
    sns.boxplot(data=df, x='not.fully.paid', y=col, hue='not.fully.paid', ax=ax, palette='Set2', legend=False)
    ax.set_title(f'{col} by Default Status')
    ax.set_xlabel('not.fully.paid')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('lc_factors_by_default.png', dpi=120)
plt.show()

Reading: loans that were not fully paid tend to have noticeably lower fico scores, higher int.rate (consistent with LendingClub's own risk-based pricing — riskier borrowers are charged more), and somewhat higher inq.last.6mths (more recent credit inquiries, a common early-warning signal of financial stress). dti and revol.util show a similar but weaker pattern.

3. Additional Feature Engineering — Correlation-Based Feature Reduction¶

In [10]:
corr_matrix = df_transformed.drop(columns=['not.fully.paid']).corr()

plt.figure(figsize=(14, 11))
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0, linewidths=0.4,
            annot_kws={'size': 7})
plt.title('Correlation Heatmap — All Features')
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('lc_correlation_heatmap.png', dpi=120)
plt.show()
In [11]:
# Identify pairs of features with strong correlation (|r| > 0.7), a common threshold for
# flagging problematic multicollinearity before modeling
strong_corr_pairs = []
for i in range(len(corr_matrix.columns)):
    for j in range(i):
        val = corr_matrix.iloc[i, j]
        if abs(val) > 0.7:
            strong_corr_pairs.append((corr_matrix.columns[i], corr_matrix.columns[j], round(val, 3)))

print("Feature pairs with |correlation| > 0.7:")
for pair in strong_corr_pairs:
    print(pair)

Feature pairs with |correlation| > 0.7:
('fico', 'int.rate', np.float64(-0.715))

Finding: only one feature pair exceeds the |r| > 0.7 threshold: fico and int.rate (r = -0.715) — which makes intuitive sense, since LendingClub explicitly prices interest rates based on the borrower's credit risk, and FICO score is a primary input to that risk assessment. Since these two variables are largely encoding the same underlying risk signal, we drop the one with the weaker individual correlation to the target (not.fully.paid) and keep the other, avoiding redundant signal being fed into the network twice.

In [12]:
# Drop the more redundant member of each strongly-correlated pair (keeping the more directly interpretable one)
cols_to_drop = []
for f1, f2, corr_val in strong_corr_pairs:
    # keep whichever of the two has a stronger individual correlation with the target
    target_corr_f1 = abs(df_transformed[f1].corr(df_transformed['not.fully.paid']))
    target_corr_f2 = abs(df_transformed[f2].corr(df_transformed['not.fully.paid']))
    drop_col = f2 if target_corr_f1 >= target_corr_f2 else f1
    if drop_col not in cols_to_drop:
        cols_to_drop.append(drop_col)

print(f"Dropping {len(cols_to_drop)} redundant feature(s): {cols_to_drop}")

df_final = df_transformed.drop(columns=cols_to_drop)
print(f"Final feature set shape: {df_final.shape}")

Dropping 1 redundant feature(s): ['fico']
Final feature set shape: (9578, 18)

4. Deep Learning Model — Keras with TensorFlow Backend¶

In [13]:
X = df_final.drop(columns=['not.fully.paid'])
y = df_final['not.fully.paid']

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=y
)

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

print(f"Train shape: {X_train_scaled.shape}  |  Test shape: {X_test_scaled.shape}")
print(f"Train target balance:\n{y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).round(4)}")

In [14]:
class_weights_array = compute_class_weight('balanced', classes=np.unique(y_train), y=y_train)
class_weight_dict = {0: class_weights_array[0], 1: class_weights_array[1]}
print("Class weights:", class_weight_dict)

Class weights: {0: np.float64(0.5952454940957116), 1: np.float64(3.124796084828711)}

As with the class imbalance in Section 2a, we use class weighting during training so the loss function penalizes missed defaults more heavily, without altering the underlying data distribution.

In [15]:
n_features = X_train_scaled.shape[1]

model = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Input(shape=(n_features,)),
    layers.Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    layers.BatchNormalization(),
    layers.Dropout(0.3),

    layers.Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    layers.Dropout(0.2),

    layers.Dense(16, activation='relu'),

    layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

model.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=[keras.metrics.AUC(name='auc'), keras.metrics.Precision(name='precision'),
             keras.metrics.Recall(name='recall')]
)

model.summary()

Architecture rationale: with a smaller feature set (13-ish features after transformation and correlation-based reduction) and a moderate dataset size (~9,578 rows), a compact funnel network (64 -> 32 -> 16 -> 1) is appropriate — a much larger network would be prone to overfitting on a dataset this size. BatchNormalization and Dropout are included after the first, widest layer to regularize training, and AUC/Precision/Recall are tracked throughout given the class imbalance noted earlier.

early_stop = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
    monitor='val_auc', mode='max', patience=10, restore_best_weights=True
)

history = model.fit(
    X_train_scaled, y_train,
    validation_split=0.15,
    epochs=100,
    batch_size=64,
    class_weight=class_weight_dict,
    callbacks=[early_stop],
    verbose=2
)

Evaluation on the held-out test set¶

In [18]:
y_prob = model.predict(X_test_scaled, verbose=0).ravel()
y_pred = (y_prob >= 0.5).astype(int)

test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob)
avg_precision = average_precision_score(y_test, y_prob)

print(f"Test AUC: {test_auc:.4f}")
print(f"Test Average Precision (PR-AUC): {avg_precision:.4f}")
print()
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=['Fully Paid', 'Not Fully Paid']))

Interpreting the results: as in Section 2a, accuracy alone would be a misleading headline metric on this ~84:16 imbalanced target. The evaluation instead centers on ROC-AUC (ranking quality across all thresholds) and Recall on the "Not Fully Paid" class (the business-critical number — missing a true default costs LendingClub far more than an unnecessary manual review of a loan that would have been repaid). As with the earlier Home Credit project, a lender would typically want to move the decision threshold below 0.5 to trade some Precision for higher Recall on defaults, depending on the actual cost of a missed default versus a false alarm.

5. Summary¶

Key takeaways:

  1. Feature transformation: the single categorical column (purpose) was one-hot encoded into discrete numerical features.
  2. EDA: confirmed the ~84:16 class imbalance; found that lower fico, higher int.rate, and more recent credit inquiries are all associated with a higher chance of default — consistent with financial intuition and with LendingClub's own risk-based interest-rate pricing. small_business loans and loans that failed LendingClub's own credit-policy check default at noticeably higher rates.
  3. Correlation-based feature reduction: checked pairwise feature correlations and removed redundant features (keeping the one more predictive of the target), reducing dimensionality before modeling.
  4. Deep learning model: a compact Keras/TensorFlow neural network (64 → 32 → 16 → 1) with batch normalization, dropout, and class-weighted training was used to predict default risk, evaluated primarily via AUC and Recall on the minority (default) class rather than raw accuracy.

Possible next steps: threshold tuning to match LendingClub's actual cost structure for missed defaults vs. false alarms, and comparing this deep learning model against simpler baselines (e.g., logistic regression, gradient boosting) to confirm the added complexity of a neural network is justified on a dataset this size.
